As Darren Woods mentioned, it is a channel for us. It is an opportunity or a way for us to maximize the value of our assets and the products that we sell. It gives us the optionality and the flexibility, and it particularly is manifest when you see things like today, when those trade flows shift. Our ability to then place products where they generate the most value, where they're most needed, the ability to place feedstocks in our refineries is a true differentiator for us. It's, again, all around this desire to maximize the assets and the value of our fully integrated value chain. Your next question will come from Jason Gabelman with TD Cowen. Your line is open. Please go ahead. Yeah. Hey, thanks for taking my questions. In the spirit of kind of exploring the portfolio beyond 2030, there's been reports both on your interest in Venezuela, which maybe has moved to the fore a bit more quickly than we had anticipated earlier in the year, and then also interest in expanding your operational footprint in Kazakhstan with the Kashagan project. So I was hoping you could just touch on your aspirations in both of those regions. Thanks. Yeah, sure. Happy to do that, Jason. I think, first of all, I would just caution everybody to take what's reported in the press with respect to Venezuela and ourselves with a little pinch of salt. I think sometimes there's maybe a little more exuberance than is warranted. In my mind, we're not behind or ahead of anything that I talked about going all the way back to January. We recognize, and I think that the world does, that Venezuela has a lot of resource. It's a challenged resource with respect to the qualities of that crude and the challenges of producing it. We absolutely see a need for that resource at some point in the future, but it's going to have to be produced and developed at a very competitive cost in order for it to compete on the world markets. That's going to require a scale and a technology capability and an operating capability that, frankly, very few companies have. We believe we have advantages in that space, and therefore ultimately will have a role. But, like I said earlier, it's going to require some substantial changes to the way things have historically been done in Venezuela. There is progress being made on those areas, working on fiscal regimes, working on legal regimes, working on investor protections, a number of things that are kind of in progress, but there's a way to go. I would just tell you, we're going to make sure that before we commit, that those are in place and we have confidence that we have a viable project that's sustainable and will generate the returns required to compete in our portfolio. I expect that to take time. We're working our way through it. We're not in a rush. We think that opportunities are going to be there for a while, and so we're trying to be methodical and thorough, and I'd say that's how it's working. With Kazakhstan, I just think, again, another potential opportunity. I think some of the constructs of the past have introduced a lot of complexity that hasn't allowed us and the industry to effectively develop those resources. We've left a lot of, I think, potential trapped. As these ventures kind of proceed, we think there's an opportunity to optimize that, and we're working with the partners there, we're working with the governments to see if we can't find a better win-win proposition for all the players there, including ourselves and for the government of Kazakhstan. We see a line of sight to that, but again, it'll take time to work our way through, and we've got some very constructive discussions happening today, and hopefully those will come to fruition sometime here in the near future. But it's a work in progress. Your next question will come from Sam Margolin with Wells Fargo. Your line is open. Please go ahead. Hello. Thanks for taking the question. I guess continuing on the theme of bringing an advantage to wherever you are, on the inorganic side, in the industry, transaction pace is picking up. Some of what's going on is probably small for you, but nevertheless, it seems fairly active. You're moving to a place where the balance sheet has a tremendous amount of capacity. Just wondering what your latest thoughts are on the capability to do something inorganic and deliver some of your proprietary edge to an asset that could stand for some improvement. Yeah. Well, thank you, Sam. I agree with your thesis and the way you're thinking about it. Frankly, going all the way back when we started this effort to really focus on these core capabilities, tried to build an advantage so we can improve our own operations and organic investment opportunities as well as inorganic ones. Our view is this lever was going to help us across the board. Frankly, as we look forward with the ambitions that we have to grow earnings and cash flow, we're going to need every lever available to us. So we're going to need exploration and going out and finding new resources. We're going to need the ability to optimize the resources that we have and maximize recovery, and then we're going to need to take advantage of inorganic opportunities that are value-accretive to the portfolio. I would tell you we're actively working all aspects of that because we recognize that all aspects are going to be required. So I think that opportunity is there. Obviously, it's a function of finding the right partner organization and one where you can arrive at a mutually agreed value share. But I definitely think there's something there, and we're continuing to work it. My suspicion is that as we get better and better and realize the advantages, the more deal space opens up and potentially more opportunity. But that's kind of, I'd say, an evolving space. Sam, maybe, I mean, you referenced this in your question, that we bring a set of unique competitive advantages that inherently create deal space. If you just look back on the prior acquisitions we've done recently, taking, for an example, with Pioneer, and we've been able to double the synergies of that acquisition from $2 billion to $4 billion a year. You look at Denbury and the acquisition of the Green Pipeline and the impact that's having on our approach to building out a CCS business. I mean, we now have, I think, 11 MTA under contract across eight customers. So, the history and the experience we've had is we've been able to demonstrate bringing those advantages, those things that we do really well, more unique than anyone, and we're able to create additional value to shareholders. Again, as Darren mentioned, certainly a tool that we'll continue to look at, but we have to be patient and find those opportunities where we can bring that value and accrete additional value for shareholders. Your next question will come from James West with Melius Research. Your line is open. Please go ahead. Something we've been looking into and thinking more about, and it's occurred over a longer period of time, is as Exxon has evolved over the last decade or two, you've taken much more of an operatorship or a control stake in projects. I'm assuming that's something that you've done, you've tried to do this, but you've also proven that you have that operational expertise. So, curious if you could just talk about, has this been a disciplined approach? Is this the approach going forward? Is this how you're thinking about the business? Or are we thinking about it correctly, that you have meaningfully increased your operatorship percentage over time? Yeah. Thanks, James. You're spot on. I think what you're observing is a reflection of the approach that we're moving towards, and we won't be able to execute it in all circumstances. But if you go back to the value thesis that we've been executing for the last decade, it's really, we are uniquely positioned with a scale that frankly none of our competitors have, and a portfolio of businesses with the synergies that none of our competitors have. As we started transforming the organization and creating value chains and then centralizing these core capabilities, so think technology, projects, and operations, we're now, for the first time in the corporation's history, capable of learning, taking all the best practices and learnings across our portfolio and in projects, whether those practices came from our traditional or historical refining projects organization or upstream project organization or chemical projects organization, or in fact, from our technology company. Those are all now in one organization, and that organization is taking the best of the thinking that we have across the company, irrespective of what business or function it was in, and applying that to the portfolio. For projects, which was the first organization where we started that, we've seen huge benefits and improvements in bringing the best thinking of ExxonMobil across our entire portfolio together and to bring those to bear on our toughest challenges. Technology was the second core organization that we did that, and again, we're seeing the real benefits of that, where rather than organize ourselves around the company and the businesses that we've set up, instead organize ourselves around the capabilities and then apply the best capabilities to the hardest problems. I'll give you just one quick example of how that paid off. The lightweight proppant that we're now seeing deployed throughout the Permian and bringing significant value, that was refining technologists who work on cokers applying their understanding of coke morphology to a challenge in the upstream organization and coming up with a brand new proppant, a cost-effective proppant. We wouldn't have had that without the technology, and we're seeing that again across all aspects of technology, and so that's bringing a huge advantage. Then we just, for the first time ever in the company, established one operating organization so that people running LNG facilities are working with and collaborating with people who run refineries or traditional chemical plants, and same with our offshore platforms. Today, we're seeing a great mix across that, and that learning is unique to ExxonMobil in the industry, and we see huge value from that. Then in order to realize that value, we've got to be in a position where we can bring it to bear on the projects that we're engaged with, which means we need to be an operator. In order to justify that effort and that allocation of resource, we need to be an operator with a significant level, a significant share of the project. That's how we're thinking about it. We think we bring real value there, we bring value to our partners, and we bring value to the resource owners. To date, that's really beginning to demonstrate itself. Yeah, maybe I'll just add, Darren, that desire for more direct control over operations and project execution really is the direct result of the confidence we have in the organization. We've talked about the operational excellence this quarter, but you look at, Darren mentioned global projects and their performance over time, we're executing double the number of mega projects than any of our IOCs, and that performance is yielding results. They're delivering projects at 20% lower cost and 20% faster schedule time. Part of this desire to take more direct control of operations and project execution is the organization continues to perform really well in those areas. We have time for one more question. Our final question comes from John Royall with Piper Sandler. Your line is open. Please go ahead. Hi, good morning. Thanks for taking my question. My question's on the Middle East. You guided to a 350 KBD impact unchanged in 4Q, and I know a lot of that is wrapped up in Qatar LNG where you've had some damage. Can you speak to the egress side in the UAE in terms of what you've been able to get out of the strait or divert barrels elsewhere if applicable, and just how that's evolved over the past quarter or so since the MOU ended? Sure, yeah. Thanks for the question, John. I think you are right. The impact that we are seeing from a volume standpoint is concentrated in Qatar and the loss of those trains and then the inability to flow at the rates and transport LNG at the rates we were prior to the conflict. UAE production has been back up again, essentially consistent with where we have historically been. The sales, though, have been deferred just based on the constraints. What we are seeing is, while the production is being booked, the realization of that production is delayed simply as a function of the logistics and the ability to move the barrels out. We are working to basically improve upon that. I know the UAE is very focused on developing more logistics routes to get barrels out, and we are working with them on that. Our expectation is with time, we will start to see the sales revenue catch up with the production numbers. But that today is certainly impacting us in the short term. Thanks for the question. All right. Thanks, John. Thanks, everybody, for joining this call and for your questions. We are going to post the transcript of this call to the investor section of our website by early next week, and have a good weekend. title: Exxon earnings: $19B cash haul comes with a catch - TradingView
content: ExxonMobil’s (XOM) latest earnings give investors something more useful than another headline about soaring oil profits: a test of how much cash the business can generate – and how much shareholders should expect to keep receiving. The energy giant reported third-quarter net income of $15.4 billion on October 30, with adjusted earnings of $4.23 per share beating the $4.08 LSEG consensus. Refining strength helped drive the result, as disruptions to global fuel supplies boosted margins. But the investment question extends beyond this quarter’s windfall: what survives when those conditions ease? Refining reveals why Exxon is more than an oil-price bet Exxon’s Energy Products segment earned $7.17 billion, edging past the $7.09 billion generated by its upstream business. Compared with Q2, fuel-making profits increased while upstream earnings declined. That divergence illustrates the value of owning businesses across the energy supply chain. For investors, crude prices alone therefore offer an incomplete guide to Exxon’s prospects. Refiners earn money from the spread between feedstock costs and finished-fuel prices; that spread can strengthen even when oil-production earnings weaken. Integration provides another source of earnings, but unusually favorable refining conditions can also flatter consolidated profitability. Investors assessing future earnings should watch diesel margins alongside crude prices, rather than assume every business will keep contributing at today’s pace. XOM’s cash cushion is substantial – but timing helped Exxon generated $19.1 billion in free cash flow and distributed $9.4 billion through dividends and buybacks. Its reported cash generation therefore covered those payments roughly twice over, leaving considerable financial flexibility. However, working-capital movements contributed approximately $2.2 billion to operating cash flow. Excluding those movements, operating cash flow fell to $23.4 billion from $25.7 billion in the preceding quarter, even as the headline measure increased. That distinction matters because inventory, receivables and payment timing can shift cash between reporting periods without representing a lasting improvement in earning power. Shareholders still received strong cash backing for their payouts. But annualizing the headline free-cash-flow figure would risk treating a favorable quarterly movement as recurring income. The more revealing test is cash generation across several quarters, after investment needs and working-capital swings. Exxon also announced $20 billion of share repurchases for 2027, subject to reasonable market conditions. The qualification deserves attention: it preserves management’s ability to respond if the operating environment deteriorates. Buybacks can increase remaining shareholders’ ownership and support per-share earnings, but their investment value depends on the price paid and the cash available through the cycle. A large authorization alone cannot establish that shares are cheap. For prospective buyers, the strongest takeaway is Exxon’s capacity to convert favorable markets into financial flexibility. The unresolved question is how much of that capacity persists under more ordinary conditions. Friday’s results make cash coverage, refining profitability and capital allocation the measures to watch next. Those will help distinguish a stronger underlying business from a particularly lucrative quarter. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. Select reference data provided by FactSet. Uncertainty and fear continue to dominate the stock market as oil prices remain high amid Middle East tensions. Investors are also closely watching the upcoming U.S. midterm elections to assess how the results could influence stock market performance. With the market expected to remain highly volatile, it is advisable for investors to increase their allocation to low-beta stocks. Companies that seem good bets now are BP plc BP, ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM, ConocoPhillips COP and Eni S.p.A. E. Beta measures the volatility or risk of a particular asset compared to the market. In other words, beta measures the extent of a security's price movement relative to the market. In this article, we are considering the S&P 500 as the market. If a stock has a beta of 1, then the price of the stock will move with the market. So, the stock is more volatile than the market if its beta is more than 1. In the same way, the stock is not as volatile as the market if its beta is less than 1. For example, if the market offers a return of 20%, a stock with a beta of 3 will return 60%, which is overwhelming. Similarly, when the market slips 20%, the stock will sink 60%, which is devastating. We have taken a beta between 0 and 0.6 as our prime criterion for screening stocks that are less volatile than the market. However, this should not be the only factor to be considered while selecting a winning strategy. We need to take into account other parameters that can add value to the portfolio. Integrated energy company ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM) fell short of the market's revenue expectations in Q3 2026, but revenue rose 29.6% year on year to $110.5 billion. Its GAAP profit of $3.72 per share was 7% below analysts' consensus estimates. For more on ExxonMobil, read our full research report. Revenue $110.5 billion vs S&P analysts' consensus estimates of $118.3 billion (29.6% year-on-year growth, 6.6% miss) EPS (GAAP) $3.72 vs analysts' consensus estimates of $4.00 (7% miss) Operating margin 19.2%, up from 12.9% in the same quarter last year Cyclical industries such as energy can make mediocre companies look strong for a time, but a long-term view reveals which businesses can actually withstand and adapt to changing conditions. Over the last five years, ExxonMobil grew its revenue at a mediocre 9.8% compounded annual growth rate, falling short of the benchmark for the energy upstream and integrated energy sector. Within energy, a single time frame, even a long one, only sheds light on how well a company rode the last commodity cycle. An even longer, ten-year view helps assess whether a company compounds through cycles. ExxonMobil's annualized revenue growth of 5.8% over the last ten years is below its five-year trend, but the results were still good. While looking at revenue is important, it can also introduce noise around commodity prices and M&A. Analyzing drivers of revenue, on the other hand, highlights what is happening inside the asset base and whether the economic footprint of a company is expanding. Over the last two years, ExxonMobil's oil production averaged 9.9% year-on-year growth. On the other hand, its natural gas production averaged 1.1% year-on-year declines. This quarter, ExxonMobil generated a strong 29.6% year-on-year revenue growth rate, but its $110.5 billion of revenue fell short of Wall Street's high expectations. Its oil production fell by 3% year on year. Adjusted EBITDA margin captures the operating profitability of an energy producer by removing accounting effects related to depletion and capitalized drilling costs. It reveals how much cash the asset base generates before capital structure and reinvestment requirements shape reported earnings. ExxonMobil was profitable over the last five years but held back by its large cost base. Its average EBITDA margin of 22.5% was weak for an upstream and integrated energy business. ExxonMobil's EBITDA margin may have fluctuated slightly, but it has generally stayed the same over the last year. This raises questions about the company's expense base because its revenue growth should have given it leverage on its fixed costs, resulting in better economies of scale and profitability. In Q3, ExxonMobil generated an EBITDA margin of 31.5%, up 11 percentage points year on year. This increase was a positive development and shows it was more efficient. Adjusted EBITDA beat Wall Street's consensus estimates by 17.1%. ExxonMobil's revenue and EPS both fell short of Wall Street's consensus estimates, making this a weaker quarter with few positives. Shares edged higher 1.9% to $186.82 immediately after the report. For investors considering ExxonMobil right now, the latest quarter matters, but not as much as longer-term business quality and valuation. title: XOM Q3 Earnings & Revenues Beat Estimates on Strong Refining Margins - TradingView
content: ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM reported third-quarter 2026 adjusted earnings of $4.23 per share, beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $3.90 per share by 8.5%. The bottom line increased from the year-ago figure of $1.88 per share. Revenues of $113.16 billion topped the consensus estimate of $103 billion by 9.9% and increased 32.7% year over year from $85.29 billion. GAAP earnings per share (EPS) rose to $3.72 from $1.76 in the year-ago quarter. The strong results were primarily driven by record refining margins, operational efficiency and optimization activities. Higher profitability was supported by strong Energy Products performance despite disruptions in Middle East production. Upstream production totaled 4,496 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day (Mboe/d). ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation Quote ExxonMobil's Energy Products segment generated adjusted earnings of $9.05 billion in the third quarter of 2026. The segment benefited from exceptionally strong refining margins as global supply disruptions constrained the availability of gasoline, diesel and other refined products. Refining capacity disruptions in Russia and the Middle East tightened product markets, supporting stronger margins. XOM's global refining network and optimization capabilities helped capture favorable market conditions. The company achieved record global diesel yields and North American diesel volumes during the first nine months of 2026. Energy Products sales totaled 5,753 thousand barrels per day (Mbd) in third-quarter. Global refinery throughput reached 3,735 Mbd, supported by strong utilization across the company's refining network. XOM's Upstream segment reported adjusted earnings of $7.31 billion in the third quarter. Higher commodity prices supported earnings, while production disruptions in the Middle East and increased depreciation associated with advantaged investments weighed on performance. The company continued benefiting from production growth in Guyana and the Permian Basin. Permian output remained above 1.8 MMboe/d, supported by technology-driven improvements in recovery and capital efficiency. Middle East disruptions constrained production availability. The company reported regional production of approximately 550 Mboe/d, while shipping restrictions delayed recognition of certain sales and revenues in the UAE. XOM Sees Support From Chemical & Specialty Products ExxonMobil's Chemical Products segment generated adjusted earnings of $725 million during the quarter. Record operational reliability and North American feedstock advantages supported profitability, although weaker chemical margins presented challenges. Chemical Products sales totaled 4,888 thousand metric tons. Strong operational execution and increased demand for high-value products in Asia Pacific supported the business despite elevated regional product availability and higher feedstock costs. Specialty Products contributed adjusted earnings of $1.28 billion, supported by favorable basestock margins. Sales volumes totaled 1,737 thousand metric tons, while the company's focus on differentiated products and structural cost reductions supported profitability. ExxonMobil's Expenses Rise Despite Efficiency Gains XOM's total costs and other deductions increased 23.6% to $91.93 billion from $74.36 billion. Crude oil and product purchases rose 37.1% to $65.72 billion, reflecting the higher cost of materials purchased during the quarter. Production and manufacturing expenses increased 11.1% to $11.22 billion from $10.09 billion. Depreciation and depletion expenses rose 5.1% to $6.80 billion, reflecting the impact of the company's expanding asset base and investments. Selling, general and administrative expenses declined 11.7% to $2.68 billion from $3.03 billion, providing some cost relief. ExxonMobil's cumulative structural cost savings have reached $16.9 billion since 2019, reflecting continued efforts to improve operational efficiency. ExxonMobil's income before taxes increased 94.3% to $21.24 billion from $10.93 billion. The improvement reflected stronger revenue generation and favorable refining conditions, which more than offset increased operating expenses. Income tax expenses rose 64.8% to $5.21 billion from $3.16 billion, reflecting higher taxable earnings. Despite the increased tax burden, net income attributable to ExxonMobil surged 104.2% to $15.41 billion from $7.55 billion in the year-ago quarter. The company's overall profitability benefited from its integrated operating model, which helped capture stronger refining margins amid global supply constraints. XOM generated $25.65 billion in operating cash flow during the third quarter, supported by strong earnings and operational performance. Free cash flow totaled $19.11 billion, reflecting cash generation after investments and other cash-flow adjustments. The company returned $9.4 billion to shareholders, including $4.3 billion in dividends and $5.1 billion in share repurchases. Cash capital expenditures totaled $7 billion, reflecting continued investments in advantaged projects and long-term production capacity. ExxonMobil expects full-year 2026 Permian production of approximately 1.8 MMboe/d. Its fifth Guyana production vessel is scheduled to begin operations late in the fourth quarter. Middle East disruptions are expected to keep approximately 350 Mboe/d offline. Higher scheduled maintenance in Product Solutions could affect performance. XOM expects full-year capital expenditures of $27-$29 billion and fourth-quarter corporate and financing expenses of $500-$700 million. The company plans $20 billion in share repurchases in 2027, subject to market conditions. ExxonMobil currently sports a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy). Author:

                      Updated on: 2026-10-30 ExxonMobil (NYSE: XOM) heads into its third-quarter 2026 earnings release, with refining margins expected to deliver its largest positive contribution to earnings. Its October 16 filing estimates a $4.5 billion improvement in Energy Products margins versus the second quarter, offset by a $1.3 billion earnings drag from lower liquids prices. The reported change in company-wide profitability will depend on the refining benefit and other operating and accounting effects. Consensus forecasts put earnings at $4.03 per share and revenue at $106.02 billion, up from $1.88 and $85.29 billion a year earlier. XOM closed at $183.29 on October 29, following a rally. ExxonMobil had not published its Q3 results on the investor-relations page when checked, so company disclosures and forecasts remain separate. Earnings expectations: Q3 consensus forecasts stand at $4.03 per share and $106.02 billion in revenue, both estimates, not reported results. Refining profitability: ExxonMobil estimates a $4.5 billion quarter-on-quarter improvement in Energy Products margins, its largest favourable disclosed market factor. Upstream pressure: Lower liquids prices are expected to reduce upstream earnings by $1.3 billion, partly offset by $300 million from natural gas prices. Shareholder returns: Q2 free cash flow of $17.2 billion covered $9.4 billion of dividends and repurchases, providing a benchmark for Q3. XOM stock: Shares rallied ahead of the results, while recurring profitability and cash generation remain measures of operating performance. Consensus forecasts imply earnings-per-share growth of about 114% versus the prior year and revenue growth of roughly 24%. Those rates are calculations based on the forecast comparison figures, not ExxonMobil’s own Q3 guidance. The EPS growth comparison assumes the forecast and year-earlier figures use consistent accounting measures. The $4.03 estimate would represent a 14.5% increase from Q2 adjusted earnings per share of $3.52, provided the forecast and reported measures are comparable. ExxonMobil reported $14.5 billion in Q2 GAAP profit and $14.7 billion in adjusted earnings, excluding specified non-operational items and estimated timing effects. The two measures distinguish reported profitability from earnings adjusted for those items. ExxonMobil’s Energy Products business refines crude oil and sells products such as gasoline and diesel, which have different pricing dynamics. Refining margins improve when product prices rise relative to feedstock and processing costs, allowing the business to earn more from its output. Lower crude realisations can reduce upstream earnings while supporting parts of the refining business during the same quarter. The company’s filing estimates a $4.5 billion benefit from Energy Products margins, offset by a $600 million decline from Chemical Products margins and supplemented by a $500 million improvement in Speciality Products margins. Together, these changes produce an estimated $4.4 billion favourable margin effect across the three businesses, before other operating and accounting factors. The calculation measures selected quarter-over-quarter changes rather than additional net profit because it must also include commodity-price movements, operational costs, and other adjustments. Source: ExxonMobil’s October 16 Form 8-K; selected estimated drivers, not Q3 results. The preliminary filing separately identifies approximately $2.5 billion in unfavourable Q3 timing effects, including $1.9 billion assigned to Energy Products. Such effects largely arise when derivatives are valued before the related physical commodity transactions appear in earnings, potentially creating temporary differences between accounting results and commercial performance. Q2 also contained timing adjustments, so the full Q3 amount does not represent a new quarter-over-quarter loss without comparing the corresponding adjustments in both periods. ExxonMobil reported Q2 upstream earnings of $7.9 billion under GAAP and $9.2 billion on an adjusted basis, a $1.3 billion difference between the two profitability measures. Permian output exceeded 1.8 million oil-equivalent barrels per day, while total company production averaged 4.514 million barrels of oil equivalent per day. Regional production growth does not necessarily translate into a proportional increase in total company output. For Q3, the filing estimates that lower liquids prices will reduce upstream earnings by $1.3 billion and higher natural gas prices will add $300 million. It also lists a $900 million unfavourable change from other upstream factors such as entitlements, sales timing and tax impacts. These estimates show that upstream profitability depends on realised selling prices and other financial effects alongside production volumes. Guyana offers a separate source of prospective growth, with ExxonMobil’s fifth offshore production vessel scheduled to start up in Q4, as announced in its Q2 update. The project is expected to add 250,000 barrels per day of production capacity, although capacity is not the same as immediate realised output. Start-up timing and operating costs will determine its near-term contribution, while oil prices will influence the revenue earned on additional barrels. ExxonMobil reported Q2 operating cash flow of $23.6 billion and free cash flow of $17.2 billion, a non-GAAP measure reflecting cash generated after investment-related flows. It returned $4.3 billion in dividends and $5.1 billion through share repurchases, for combined shareholder distributions of $9.4 billion. These figures provide a basis for comparing shareholder distributions with Q3 cash generation. The $7.8 billion remainder is not equivalent to unrestricted cash, since financing needs and balance-sheet decisions still have to be considered. Q3 cash flow will show whether additional refining earnings translated into greater financial flexibility after capital spending. XOM gained 13.3% over the month leading up to the earnings report, reflecting a substantial increase in its share price. Published analyst consensus targets of $167.70 and $179.41 both sit below the $183.29 October 29 close, based on different analyst samples and reporting dates. These targets reflect analysts’ valuation estimates rather than a determination of ExxonMobil’s intrinsic value. The company’s recurring earnings capacity provides a basis for assessing its valuation under less favourable energy-market conditions. Production efficiency, lower structural costs and additional profitable output could support future earnings even if refining margins retreat from elevated levels. Without corresponding improvements in these areas, earnings from elevated refining margins may not hold up in subsequent quarters. Overall, ExxonMobil’s preliminary figures show a substantial refining benefit, but the disclosed offsets prevent a reliable company-wide earnings forecast based on that margin improvement alone. Its Q2 cash generation and expanding production assets provide clear benchmarks for assessing the next set of results. The October 30 release will establish whether the expected financial improvements translated into stronger adjusted earnings, segment profitability and free cash flow. title: Chevron and Exxon hit all-time highs as refining profits soar in reaction to Iran and Ukraine wars - CNBC
content:
Chevron and ExxonMobil on Friday reported profits that soared in the third quarter, as their U.S. refineries ramped up production to full capacity to take advantage of high diesel fuel prices. Chevron shares are up nearly 2% while Exxon is more than 1% higher. Both touched all-time highs Friday. The world is facing a fuel crisis as Ukraine, Iran and Houthi militants attack refineries in Russia and the Middle East, reducing global capacity by millions of barrels per day. Importers have increasingly turned to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries for diesel supplies as a consequence. ExxonMobil’s profits doubled to $15.4 billion, or $3.72 a share, compared to $7.5 billion, or $1.76 a share, in the same period in 2025. When adjusted for one-time items, it posted earnings of $4.23 a share, soundly beating Wall Street’s expectations. “Refining capacity is very tight today,” Exxon CEO Darren Woods told CNBC in an interview. “Frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth [with] very inelastic demand.” U.S. diesel stood at a national average of $6.32 per gallon on Friday, an increase of more than 70% compared to the same period last year, according to AAA. Prices in the U.S. hit a record high in September. Chevron’s net income surged nearly 200% to $9.9 billion, or $5.06 a share, compared to $3.5 billion, or $1.82 a share, in the same period last year. When adjusted for one-time items, it reported earnings of $5.28 per share, also beating the Street’s expectations of $4.89. “The system is under stress,” Chevron CEO Mike Wirth told CNBC in an interview. “We remain in an environment that is fairly fragile.” Here’s what Chevron and Exxon earned, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG: High profits from the largest oil companies at a time of war is politically controversial. President Donald Trump said in August that Chevron and Exxon “were making too much money based on a shortage.” The supply disruption began in March after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran. Profits from Chevron’s refining division surged more than 300% to $4.9 billion compared to $1.1 billion in the same period in 2025. Its oil and gas production generated earnings of $5.7 billion, up 70% from $3.3 billion in the year-ago period. Chevron’s U.S. refineries processed record amounts of crude oil at just above 1 million barrels per day, as the facilities ran at 98% capacity. Diesel and jet fuel yields rose more than 10%, Wirth said. Exxon’s refining division generated profits of about $7.2 billion in the quarter, outpacing its production business’ earnings of about $7.1 billion. Its refining profits have surged nearly 200% to $11.4 billion so far this year compared to $4 billion during the first nine months of 2025. Exxon’s Gulf Coast refineries operated at 100% capacity utilization. Those refineries produced “record volumes of diesel” in the quarter, Woods said. Chevron’s oil and gas production actually declined slightly to 3.9 million barrels per day compared to about 4 million bpd in the same period last year. The decline was in its international segment due in part to the conflict in the Middle East, while output was largely flat in the U.S. year over year. Exxon Mobil Corp (NYSE:XOM, XETRA:XONA) reported third-quarter earnings of $15.4 billion, up from $14.5 billion in the previous quarter, as stronger refining margins and operational performance helped offset weaker upstream results. The US oil major reported GAAP earnings of $3.72 per share, while adjusted earnings reached $17.5 billion, or $4.23 per share, beating the LSEG consensus estimate of $4.08, compared with adjusted EPS of $3.52 in the second quarter. Cash flow from operating activities totalled $25.7 billion, while free cash flow reached $19.1 billion, up from $17.2 billion in the previous quarter. Energy Products was the strongest contributor to the sequential improvement, with earnings rising to $7.2 billion from $5.5 billion as higher margins and stronger operational performance supported results. ExxonMobil said its US Gulf Coast refineries achieved 100% crude unit utilisation, while diesel production reached its second-highest level on record in the region. Upstream earnings, however, fell to $7.1 billion from $7.9 billion in the second quarter, reflecting lower prices and an accelerated impact from production entitlements in Guyana. Chemical Products earnings declined to $735 million from $1.1 billion as margins weakened, while Specialty Products earnings increased to $1.3 billion from $956 million on higher basestock margins. The company reported upstream production of 4.5 million oil-equivalent barrels per day, compared with 4.51 million barrels per day in the previous quarter. ExxonMobil returned $9.4 billion to shareholders during the quarter, comprising $4.3 billion in dividends and $5.1 billion in share repurchases. The company declared a fourth-quarter dividend of $1.07 per share, payable on December 10 to shareholders registered on November 16. Chief executive Darren Woods said sustained investment, operational improvements and structural cost savings had strengthened the company's earnings capacity, while helping it increase production and meet global energy demand. ExxonMobil also said it had achieved $16.9 billion in cumulative structural cost savings since 2019 and announced plans for $20 billion in share repurchases in 2027. Jim Cramer told Mad Money viewers to swap Exxon for Chevron, and on October 30 both giants report back to back. Six numbers will reveal whether that call holds or collapses. Because the two reports land back to back, they give a clean test of Jim Cramer’s October 15 call on Mad Money. “I think Exxon’s good. I think Chevron’s better. I would make that swap unless you have some tax implications. CVX is a better way to go,” Cramer said. This year, the two stocks have moved almost in tandem. Exxon is up 48.4% year to date, and Chevron is up 47.0%. Woods also pointed to Guyana output near 900,000 barrels per day, record Permian volumes above 1.8 million oil-equivalent barrels per day, more than $9 billion returned to shareholders, and $16.3 billion in cumulative cost savings since 2019. “Stepping back, the second quarter was shaped by disruption, but defined by execution,” he said. Chevron CFO Eimear Bonner reported adjusted EPS of $6.06 and adjusted free cash flow (the cash left over after capital spending) of $15.4 billion, with only about 1% of production affected by the conflict. Mike Wirth, who spoke as chair and CEO, cited record U.S. upstream output of nearly 2.1 million barrels of oil equivalent per day and $3 billion in structural cost cuts reached six months early. “Amid geopolitical uncertainty and market volatility, Chevron delivered a strong second quarter,” Wirth said. title: ExxonMobil (XOM) Q3 earnings: what to expect - The Globe and Mail
content: Integrated energy company ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM) will be reporting results this Friday before market open. Here’s what you need to know. ExxonMobil beat analysts’ revenue expectations last quarter, reporting revenues of $116 billion, up 42.3% year on year. It was a strong quarter for the company, with a significant miss of analysts’ EPS estimates. It reported year-on-year oil production growth of 3.5%. Is ExxonMobil a buy or sell going into earnings? Read our full analysis here, it’s free for active Edge members. This quarter, the market is expecting ExxonMobil’s revenue to grow 38.7% year on year, a reversal from the 5.2% decrease it recorded in the same quarter last year. Analysts covering the company have generally reconfirmed their estimates over the last 30 days, suggesting they anticipate the business will stay the course heading into earnings. ExxonMobil has missed Wall Street’s revenue estimates multiple times over the last two years. Looking at ExxonMobil’s peers in the upstream & integrated segment, some have already reported their Q3 results, giving us a hint as to what we can expect. Cactus delivered year-on-year revenue growth of 63.2%, meeting analysts’ expectations, and ProPetro reported revenues up 20.9%, topping estimates by 14.1%. Read our full analysis of Cactus’s results here and ProPetro’s results here. There has been positive sentiment among investors in the upstream & integrated segment, with share prices up 8.3% on average over the last month. ExxonMobil is up 13.3% during the same time and is heading into earnings with an average analyst price target of $179.41 (compared to the current share price of $183.27).
